strengths: Although no contribution type is declared, this work is best assessed as Applied/Systems: its main contribution is a broad end-to-end integration of scene graphs, language/VLM agents, trajectory simulation, 3D rendering, and video diffusion. Under that framing, the system offers an unusually comprehensive set of capabilities, including open-vocabulary object grounding, insertion/removal/replacement, ego-view editing, and multi-object behavior editing.

The explicit scene-graph representation provides useful object-level control and structural preservation, while diffusion refinement addresses the visual limitations of raw 3DGS/mesh rendering. This is a sensible and potentially impactful design for controllable autonomous-driving data generation.

The proposed counterfactual behavior construction and reviewer feedback loop are technically motivated and interpretable. The latter improves overall trajectory success from 34.29% to 51.43%, while the counterfactual module rejects 93.33% of deliberately infeasible instructions.

Results on 30 Waymo scenes are consistently favorable against ChatSim and Cosmos. The reported gains are substantial in appearance alignment (82.19% versus at most 46.25%), behavior alignment (71.67% versus 32.86%), FVD, structural preservation, and traffic-violation metrics.

The supplementary material is relatively strong: it provides test scene IDs, agent prompts, behavior-generation and validation rules, runtime breakdowns, additional ablations, qualitative sequences, and candid failure cases. The qualitative results show convincing preservation and editing in both daytime and nighttime scenes.
weaknesses: The experimental evidence is narrower and less rigorous than the broad claims suggest. Evaluation uses only 30 selected Waymo scenes, explicitly favors scenes with few pedestrians, and does not report exact sample counts by editing category, variability across scenes, confidence intervals, or statistical significance. Generalization to new datasets, cameras, geographic domains, dense traffic, and adverse conditions is untested.

Several central metrics may be biased or insufficiently validated. GPT-4o is both part of the proposed pipeline and the evaluator for appearance alignment and sampled-frame traffic violations. The paper does not establish agreement of these automatic judgments with ground truth or humans. FID/FVD are also difficult to interpret on a small edited-video collection, and the 26-person preference study lacks details about trial counts, assignment, randomization, participant expertise, and uncertainty.

The strongest traffic-realism claim is undermined by the trajectory ablation: even after refinement, only 51.43% of challenging multi-object trajectories jointly satisfy behavior alignment, collision avoidance, and on-road constraints, with 22.86% collision and 14.29% off-road rates. These values conflict sharply with the much lower video-level rates in Table 1, and the paper does not reconcile the difference beyond using different instruction sets and evaluation procedures.

Baseline coverage is limited to two systems despite the related-work table listing several relevant editors. The claim of state-of-the-art performance is therefore not fully substantiated. Fairness details are also thin: “original settings” does not specify resolution, prompting, sampling budgets, or whether baselines receive equivalent map/trajectory information, and Cosmos uses a different model variant because the preferred variant requires seven cameras.

The technical novelty of the individual agents is moderate. Most components wrap existing systems—OmniRe-style reconstruction, GPT-4/4o, Hunyuan3D, LangTraj, CogVideoX, and heuristic validators—while the orchestrator largely composes predefined functions through prompting. The system integration is valuable, but claims that all three agents are novel should be qualified and compared more directly with agentic baselines such as ChatDyn and SimSplat.

The object-grounding experiment is too small to establish robust open-vocabulary grounding: it contains only 50 queries from five scenes and counts IoU greater than 0.2 as success, an unusually permissive threshold. Performance should be reported with standard mask metrics, node-identification accuracy, query-type breakdowns, and larger-scale evaluation.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite detailed prompts. The project URL is blank, no code or generated instruction set is provided, important heuristic thresholds and diffusion-training data composition are underspecified, and the pipeline depends on proprietary GPT-4/GPT-4o services. The video diffusion stage can also change an instructed vehicle’s type and color, directly weakening the claimed fine-grained controllability.

The explicit scene-graph representation is a sensible foundation for object-level control and background preservation, while trajectory and video-diffusion refinement address complementary behavioral and visual failure modes.

Reported results against Cosmos and ChatSim are strong: Table 1 shows sizable improvements in instruction alignment, FVD, structure preservation, and traffic violations. The paper also provides component ablations, test-scene IDs, agent prompts, runtime measurements, and illustrative intermediate refinement iterations.
The authors candidly show meaningful failure cases, including driving over a median and video refinement changing a green convertible into a black sedan.
weaknesses: No contribution type is declared. I assess this primarily as Applied/Systems rather than Algorithms/General because most core machinery—3DGS reconstruction, Hunyuan3D, LangTraj, GPT-4/4o, CogVideoX, and TrajectoryCrafter—is inherited. This gives appropriate credit for integration, but makes comprehensive and reliable system-level validation essential; the current evidence is not sufficient.

The central traffic-realism and multi-object claims are substantially undercut by the paper's own direct trajectory evaluation. With refinement, Table 2 reports only 51.43% overall success, with 22.86% collision and 14.29% off-road rates. This conflicts sharply with Table 1's video-level rates of 0.58% and 1.73% and with claims that the system consistently produces realistic trajectories; the manuscript does not reconcile the protocols or discrepancy.

Baseline coverage is inadequate for the breadth of the claims. Only Cosmos and ChatSim are evaluated, despite the manuscript discussing ChatDyn, DriveEditor, SceneCrafter, SimSplat, and other relevant systems. Cosmos is also a rather different pixel-space world model. There is no strong modular baseline that combines the same reconstruction and trajectory backbone without the proposed agents, making attribution of the gains difficult.

Several key metrics are insufficiently validated. GPT-4o is used within the system and as an appearance/traffic evaluator; collision and off-road judgments from sampled video frames are not calibrated against human or geometric ground truth. The monocular tracking and back-projection used for behavior alignment is underspecified. FID/FVD sample construction, sample counts, and uncertainty are omitted.

The empirical scope is narrow: 30 curated Waymo scenes, front camera only, eight-second clips, intentionally few pedestrians, and GPT-generated instructions. There is no evaluation of robustness to genuinely free-form user language, grounding ambiguity, unseen environments, longer sequences, or different datasets.

The ablations do not establish the claimed agentic contributions convincingly. Counterfactual generation improves overall success only from 47.14% to 51.43% without uncertainty analysis; the reviewer is not compared with a non-LLM iterative controller using the same validation signals; and video refinement is assessed only with FID/FVD despite the admitted risk that it changes the requested object identity.

The grounding experiment contains only 50 queries from five scenes and declares success at the very lenient IoU threshold of 0.2. It reports thresholded accuracy rather than mIoU or performance by attribute type, so the claimed open-vocabulary grounding advantage is not well established.

Reproducibility remains poor despite including prompts and scene IDs. The video-refinement training dataset, its size and split, possible overlap with test scenes, preprocessing, detailed optimization settings, API model versions, and stochastic evaluation procedures are missing. The project-page link in the manuscript is blank.

The 26-person user study lacks essential methodological details: number of judgments per participant, sampling and randomization, blinding, participant background, agreement, confidence intervals, and significance tests. Overall, the attractive qualitative examples and reported aggregate gains do not overcome the unresolved validity and evidence issues.

strengths: Although no contribution type is declared, the paper is most appropriately assessed as Applied/Systems rather than purely Algorithms/General: its main value is a well-designed integration of explicit 3D scene graphs, multimodal agents, trajectory simulation, and video diffusion into a notably broad natural-language driving-video editor.

The system supports an unusually comprehensive set of operations—open-vocabulary object grounding, removal, insertion, replacement, ego-view editing, and multi-object behavior editing—while preserving explicit object-level control.

The reported improvements over Cosmos and ChatSim are substantial and consistent across complementary criteria. In particular, appearance alignment reaches 82.19% and behavior alignment 71.67%, versus at most 46.25% and 32.86% for the baselines; FVD, structure distance, collision rate, and off-road rate also improve materially.

The paper includes useful component-level evidence: object grounding reaches 84% accuracy versus 44% and 38% for the alternatives; behavior review raises overall trajectory success from 34.29% to 51.43%; counterfactual generation rejects 93.33% of infeasible instructions; and video refinement improves both FID and FVD.

The manuscript is clear and visually effective. The supplementary material supplies exact Waymo scene IDs, agent prompts and workflows, behavior rules, runtime breakdowns, qualitative examples, and candid failure cases, which strengthens interpretability and partial reproducibility.
The explicit discussion of remaining traffic violations and diffusion-induced changes to vehicle color/type is valuable and appropriately limits the claims.
weaknesses: The evaluation is relatively small for a system making broad robustness claims: it uses only 30 Waymo scenes, one front-facing camera, eight-second clips, and deliberately selects scenes with fewer pedestrians. Generalization across datasets, geographic domains, dense traffic, adverse weather, longer sequences, and multi-camera settings is not established.

Only two end-to-end baselines are evaluated quantitatively. The rationale that they are open-source and accept natural language is reasonable, but the paper's broad state-of-the-art claims would be stronger with comparisons or controlled evaluations against more of the methods listed in Table 8, as well as stronger modular baselines.

Several evaluation details are insufficient for judging statistical reliability. The manuscript gives no confidence intervals or repeated-run variability, and the 26-person user study does not report the number of judgments per participant, randomization, blinding, agreement, or significance testing. Reference distributions and sample counts for FID/FVD are also unclear.

Some automatic metrics risk evaluator coupling: GPT-4o is used inside the proposed system and also participates in appearance and traffic-realism evaluation, while behavior assessment depends on tracking and 2D-to-world back-projection whose accuracy is not validated. Independent annotations and sensitivity checks are needed.

The behavior module remains imperfect: even after refinement, the challenging multi-object test achieves only 51.43% overall success, with 22.86% collision and 14.29% off-road rates at the trajectory level. This substantially qualifies language such as 'consistently generate realistic and accurate trajectories,' even though the final-video benchmark is stronger.

The core technical ingredients are largely existing systems—3DGS decomposition, Hunyuan3D, LangTraj, GPT-4/4o, and CogVideoX—so the originality lies mainly in orchestration and heuristic validation. The counterfactual behavior machinery is useful but covers a fairly restricted, hand-defined behavior vocabulary rather than demonstrating general language-grounded planning.

Reproducibility is constrained by proprietary GPT models and incomplete video-refinement training details, including the size and composition of the refinement dataset, data splits, and safeguards against overlap with the 30 test scenes. The abstract's project-page link is also blank in the supplied manuscript.

The approach assumes maps and original object trajectories are provided, requires roughly two hours of per-scene reconstruction, and does not model pedestrians. These assumptions limit immediate deployment for open-world safety-critical scenario generation.

strengths: The work is best assessed as an Applied/Systems contribution rather than a purely algorithmic one: it integrates explicit 3D scene decomposition, language grounding, trajectory simulation, rendering, and diffusion refinement into a broad natural-language driving-video editor supporting removal, insertion, replacement, ego-motion changes, and multi-object behavior editing.

The scene-graph representation provides useful object-level control and preserves unedited content better than purely generative video models. The qualitative examples cover daytime, nighttime, ego-motion, and multi-object scenarios.

The reported improvements over Cosmos and ChatSim are large across instruction alignment, FVD, structural preservation, and traffic-violation metrics, while the stated per-edit runtime remains comparable. The coarse-rendering comparison also suggests that the gains do not arise solely from the final diffusion model.

The paper includes relevant component studies: iterative behavior refinement raises overall trajectory success from 34.29% to 51.43%; video refinement improves FID/FVD while recovering appearance alignment; and counterfactual behavior generation rejects 93.33% of constructed infeasible instructions.

The supplementary material provides prompts, behavior rules, test scene identifiers, additional qualitative results, a downstream detection experiment, hallucination measurements, and an explicit failure case involving a median barrier. The presentation and pipeline diagrams are generally clear.
weaknesses: The central evaluation is too small and insufficiently specified for the breadth of the claims. It uses only 30 selected Waymo scenes and GPT-4-generated, human-filtered instructions. Per-edit-type sample counts, denominators, uncertainty estimates, repeated runs, and statistical significance are not reported, despite stochastic trajectory and video generation.

Several metrics have unclear or potentially biased protocols. The manuscript does not clearly define the real reference distribution and sample count used for FID/FVD. Appearance alignment and traffic violations are judged using GPT-4o, which is also used inside the proposed system; no validation of these automatic judgments against human or geometric ground truth is given. The 26-person user study lacks details on trial allocation, randomization, blinding, agreement, and confidence intervals.

The baseline coverage is limited. Only Cosmos and ChatSim appear in the principal comparison, while multiple closely related object-editing, scene-composition, and language-driven systems discussed in the paper are excluded. Requiring bounding boxes does not preclude evaluating their rendering/editing stages using identical grounded targets. Consequently, the claim of broadly outperforming prior methods is stronger than the evidence.

The reviewer-agent ablations do not establish that multimodal agentic reasoning is responsible for the gains. The behavior reviewer largely applies fixed hand-written weight-update rules, and iterative methods receive up to five generation attempts. There is no comparison against deterministic schedules, random/best-of-N sampling, parameter search, or matched-compute refinement, so improvements may reflect additional sampling and validation rather than the proposed agent design.

Reproducibility is inadequate for a systems paper. Important details of the custom CogVideoX training data and pair construction, dataset scale, optimization settings, initial and upper-bound refinement parameters, stopping behavior, and failure handling are missing. The pipeline also depends on proprietary GPT-4/GPT-4o services and several large external models, with no reported model-version sensitivity or code/release commitment.

The method assumes maps and original object trajectories are provided and requires roughly two hours of per-scene reconstruction, substantially narrowing the apparent claim of editing an input real-world video. More importantly, the behavior module achieves only 51.43% overall success on the harder multi-object test, which conflicts with language suggesting it can consistently generate realistic and accurate trajectories. The downstream detector gains are modest and lack standard augmentation controls or uncertainty. These evidence gaps slightly outweigh the otherwise promising systems contribution.

strengths: The paper presents an ambitious end-to-end system combining explicit 3D scene decomposition, language-based object grounding, multi-object trajectory generation, rendering, and diffusion refinement. It supports a broad set of useful edits, including insertion, removal, replacement, ego-motion changes, and multi-object behavior editing.

The explicit scene graph provides meaningful controllability and structural preservation compared with purely generative video models. The separation between reasoning agents and executable tools is clear and practically motivated.

The authors provide several relevant ablations and analyses, including behavior refinement, video refinement, grounding, unreasonable-instruction rejection, hallucination measurements, runtime, and a downstream object-detection experiment. Prompts and heuristic rules are also documented extensively in the supplement.

Reported results substantially exceed ChatSim and Cosmos on instruction alignment and structure preservation. The coarse-rendering comparison suggests that some gains arise from the system design rather than solely from the diffusion post-processor.

The most appropriate contribution type is Applied/Systems rather than Algorithms/General: the primary value is the integration of existing reconstruction, language, trajectory, asset-generation, and diffusion components into a capable editing system. Under that framing, integration breadth and demonstrated functionality are legitimate contributions.
weaknesses: The empirical support is too limited for the paper's broad claims. The principal evaluation uses only 30 hand-selected Waymo scenes, explicitly favors scenes with fewer pedestrians, and provides no confidence intervals, repeated runs, or statistical tests. The number and exact distribution of evaluated instructions are not reported clearly, and the reference distributions used to compute FID and FVD are unspecified. These omissions make the headline comparisons difficult to interpret reliably.

The claimed traffic realism is not convincingly established. On the more challenging 70-instruction behavior-refinement set, the complete system achieves only 51.43% overall success, with 22.86% collision and 14.29% off-road rates. This conflicts sharply with the much lower 0.58% and 1.73% rates in the main comparison, but the paper does not adequately reconcile the difference in task difficulty or evaluation protocol. A safety-relevant system that fails nearly half of the multi-object cases cannot yet support claims that it consistently generates realistic trajectories.

Several evaluation metrics risk circularity or measurement bias. GPT-4o is both a core system component and the evaluator for appearance and traffic events, without calibration against expert annotations. Behavior is recovered through tracking and back-projection, but reconstruction error and metric accuracy are not validated. The human study reports 26 participants yet omits trial counts, sampling, randomization, blinding, agreement, and significance. Consequently, the large reported gains are less persuasive than the table suggests.

The grounding experiment is small—50 queries from five scenes—and defines success using an unusually permissive IoU threshold of 0.2. The baselines also receive substantially less privileged information than the proposed agent, which uses reconstructed object nodes, trajectories, and HD-map context. Results at standard IoU thresholds and controlled comparisons isolating each information source are needed.

Novelty at the component level is modest. Most of the pipeline consists of established external systems such as 3DGS decomposition, SAM, Hunyuan3D, LangTraj, GPT-4/4o, and CogVideoX. The reviewer agents mainly adjust a few predefined guidance weights according to heuristic checks. The counterfactual behavior expansion is largely a hand-designed token mapping and compatibility table. The paper does not compare against simpler non-agentic controllers or systematic parameter-search alternatives, so it is unclear whether agent reasoning itself provides the claimed benefit.

The video-reviewer evidence is weak: adding the reviewer changes FID only from 36.83 to 36.78 and FVD from 501.84 to 493.25, while appearance alignment remains below that of the unrefined coarse video. Thus, the ablation supports recovery of some appearance fidelity but not the stronger claim that iterative review decisively optimizes both realism and preservation.

Reproducibility is insufficient for a system paper. The diffusion training data size, provenance, train/test separation, noisy-pair construction, optimization settings, agent-model versions, sampling parameters, thresholds, failure/retry policy, and API nondeterminism are not specified adequately. Dependence on proprietary GPT models further complicates reproduction. Reported editing time also excludes the roughly two-hour per-scene reconstruction and does not fully account for preprocessing or API cost.

The downstream experiment doubles the training set from 8,000 to 16,000 images and compares only against the smaller real-only set. Without a size-matched real-data or conventional-augmentation baseline, multiple seeds, and statistical uncertainty, the small AP improvements do not demonstrate that synthetic edits are uniquely beneficial.

Generality is restricted by requiring ground-truth-like object trajectories and an HD map, focusing almost exclusively on vehicles, and testing only short front-camera Waymo clips. There is no evaluation across datasets, longer videos, dense pedestrian scenes, adverse weather, map errors, or missing trajectories. The discussion acknowledges one median-barrier failure but does not adequately address the risks of using hallucinated or traffic-invalid outputs as autonomous-driving training or validation data.

strengths: Best assessed as an Applied/Systems contribution: the paper integrates an explicit 3D scene graph, natural-language orchestration, multimodal object grounding, trajectory simulation, and diffusion-based rendering into a coherent driving-video editor. This is a meaningful capability advance even though many individual components are adapted from existing models.

The system supports an unusually broad set of operations—open-vocabulary querying, removal, insertion, replacement, ego-view editing, and multi-object behavior editing—while preserving explicit object and trajectory control.

The feedback-driven design is well motivated. The behavior reviewer raises overall trajectory success from 34.29% to 51.43%, while the video reviewer recovers appearance alignment from 65.47% to 85.28% without sacrificing the photorealism gains of diffusion refinement.

Results on 30 Waymo scenes are consistently strong relative to ChatSim and Cosmos: the method substantially improves appearance and behavior alignment, FVD, structural preservation, and measured collision/off-road rates, while retaining comparable per-edit runtime.

The experimental package is broader than the main comparison alone: it includes module ablations, an agent-only comparison, an image-editing-plus-video baseline, grounding evaluation, hallucination analysis, qualitative examples, a downstream detection experiment, detailed prompts, test scene IDs, and an explicit failure case.

The presentation is clear and visually effective. The decomposition of responsibilities among agents and tools is understandable, and the supplementary implementation details make the behavior constraints and refinement mechanisms substantially more concrete.
weaknesses: Evaluation independence is the main concern. GPT-4o is used inside the proposed system and also evaluates appearance alignment and traffic violations; moreover, behavior alignment uses essentially the same heuristic logic employed by the behavior reviewer. These couplings may favor the proposed pipeline, so independent learned metrics or blinded annotation would strengthen the evidence.

The evaluation scale and diversity are limited: only 30 curated Waymo scenes are used, scenes with pedestrians are intentionally avoided, only the front camera is considered, and the method assumes maps and original object trajectories are available. Generalization to other datasets, dense pedestrian scenes, imperfect maps/tracks, or broader geographic domains is not established.

The strongest multi-object behavior ablation still achieves only 51.43% overall success, with 22.86% collision and 14.29% off-road rates. This is a material limitation for safety-critical simulation and makes claims that the system can consistently generate realistic, compliant trajectories too strong.

The human study is insufficiently documented. Although it includes 26 participants, the paper does not clearly report participant expertise, number and randomization of evaluated trials, blinding, agreement, uncertainty, or significance tests. The automatic results likewise lack confidence intervals or repeated-run variance despite stochastic agents and diffusion models.

Main baseline coverage is narrow. ChatSim and Cosmos are relevant end-to-end comparisons, but evaluation against or adaptation of additional controllable driving editors would better isolate gains from the proposed agentic design. The claimed novelty is primarily in system composition and feedback control rather than in the underlying reconstruction, trajectory, language, or video-generation models.

Reproducibility is constrained by proprietary GPT-4/GPT-4o dependencies, substantial training and reconstruction costs, and limited reporting of stochastic settings and exact evaluation prompts. The downstream detection improvement is promising but modest and lacks repeated trials or controls for additional training data/compute.
